newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: U.N. official says tensions taking toll on rights.
newsitem.headline: U.N. official says tensions taking toll on rights.

text.p: Political tensions within Cambodia's coalition government are preventing improvements in the country's critical human rights situation, U.N. rights official Thomas Hammarberg said on Tuesday.

"Tensions within the government and the inability of (the leaders) to create a cohesive government policy...have had some negative repercussions when it comes to implementation of government reforms," said Hammarberg, the special representative of the U.N. Secretary-General for Human Rights in Cambodia.

Cambodian co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen have been feuding for nearly a year, causing deep rifts in the uneasy coalition government they formed following U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.
"The power battle is always a threat when it comes to human rights," Hammarberg said at a press conference that closed a two-week visit to Cambodia.
The parties of the two premiers are preparing to challenge each other in local and national elections, scheduled for 1997 and 1998.
Hammarberg expressed disappointment that little progress had been made toward preparing for the polls, with no good reason for long delays on the formation of necessary laws and bodies.

He called the total human rights picture "alarming". He cited reports of torture by all sectors of police, forced confessions of suspects, impunity for rights offenders and a "thoroughly corrupt" court system.

In a five-day visit to the northwest province of Battambang, Hammarberg said he learned that military and police were beating confessions out of suspects with impunity, and the deaths of four prisoners were ruled suicides without sufficient investigation.
He also said he was unhappy with government inaction on the murders of four journalists and five violent attacks on journalists and newspaper offices over the past three years.

Repeated appeals to the government to address the problems -- including a five-month-old memo detailing attacks on journalists and questioning why no cases have been thoroughly investigated -- had often been ignored, he said.
Neither Hun Sen nor Ranariddh were immediately available for comment.
